passages.title: Job loses his children and wealth
passages.summary: Satan questions Job’s reasons for serving God. Four messengers report losses. Job mourns and worships. Job’s good life does not protect his family from disaster.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads the heavenly exchange as poetry about an accuser’s challenge.

passages.title: Illness and silent friends
passages.summary: Job suffers painful sores. His wife urges him to renounce God. Three friends sit silently with him. The friends first share Job’s grief before they try to explain it.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why faith should continue when expected rewards disappear.

passages.title: Job wishes he had not been born
passages.summary: Job curses the day of his birth. He asks why people in pain must keep living. His speech gives words to grief that his earlier worship did not remove.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me allows questions and faith to remain together during suffering.

passages.title: Eliphaz explains suffering through guilt
passages.summary: Eliphaz recalls Job’s help for others. He claims innocent people do not perish. Eliphaz’s claim conflicts with the opening account, which calls Job blameless.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine the friends’ claim that pain proves guilt.

passages.title: Eliphaz urges Job to accept correction
passages.summary: Eliphaz urges Job to seek God. He promises safety, children, and long life after correction. His promises assume that Job’s losses began with wrongdoing.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions the friends’ explanation that God is punishing Job.

passages.title: Job asks his friends for kindness
passages.summary: Job describes pain beyond his strength. He compares his friends to streams that disappear when needed. He asks them to show his error instead of condemning his desperate words.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks for kindness before a verdict. How could his friends answer that request?

passages.title: Job addresses God in his pain
passages.summary: Job describes sleepless nights and painful skin. He asks God to leave him alone. He keeps speaking to God while questioning why his short life receives constant scrutiny.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job speaks directly to God about pain. What does he ask God to change?

passages.title: Bildad blames wrongdoing
passages.summary: Bildad suggests Job’s children died for their sins. He promises renewed success if Job is upright. Bildad turns a family’s deaths into an accusation.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what goes wrong when friends explain pain through blame.

passages.title: Job asks who could judge his case
passages.summary: Job describes God’s power over mountains, stars, and seas. He seeks someone to hear both sides. He fears that unequal power prevents a fair hearing.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job wants someone to hear both sides. What prevents him from feeling heard?

passages.title: Job asks why his maker harms him
passages.summary: Job recalls how God formed his body and gave him life. He asks why God now opposes him. He asks for an explanation instead of accepting his friends’ verdict.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job recalls the care that formed him. Why does his present pain make that memory difficult?

passages.title: Zophar demands that Job change
passages.summary: Zophar says Job deserves worse. He promises relief if Job removes wrongdoing from his home. His confidence leaves little room to hear Job’s claim of innocence.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions Zophar’s claim that Job’s pain comes from wrongdoing.

passages.title: Job challenges his friends’ wisdom
passages.summary: Job says he understands as much as his friends. He points to robbers who live safely. He uses what he sees to challenge their claim that wrongdoing always brings immediate loss.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what Job knows about God while challenging his friends.

passages.title: Job seeks a hearing with God
passages.summary: Job accuses his friends of speaking falsely for God. He asks God to hear his case. WEB reads verse 15 as having no hope. The King James Bible reads it as trust. Both retain Job’s resolve to defend himself.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me follows the King James Bible’s reading about trusting God. WEB follows the other reading noted above.

passages.title: Job asks whether the dead live again
passages.summary: Job compares short human life with a tree that can grow again. He asks God to remember him. The question about life after death appears within his fear of losing hope.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s question about death with resurrection through Jesus Christ.

passages.title: Eliphaz condemns Job’s words
passages.summary: Eliphaz says Job’s own words prove guilt. He describes the fear and loss awaiting wicked people. Eliphaz treats Job’s protest as evidence against him.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Eliphaz treats protest as proof of guilt. What happens when listeners make that assumption?

passages.title: Job calls his friends poor comforters
passages.summary: Job says he would strengthen them if their places were reversed. He asks for a witness in heaven. He wants someone to support his case instead of adding blame.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how friends can strengthen someone instead of adding blame.

passages.title: Job sees his hope nearing the grave
passages.summary: Job describes broken plans and public shame. He asks where his hope can go. His friends’ promised bright future does not answer the darkness he experiences.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s plans have broken apart. What kind of help could reach him now?

passages.title: Bildad describes the wicked person’s ruin
passages.summary: Bildad describes traps, disease, lost children, and a forgotten name. He calls this the wicked person’s fate. His description echoes Job’s losses and deepens the accusation.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad describes the loss of a name and children. How might Job hear those words?

passages.title: Job asks for pity and a defender
passages.summary: Job describes relatives, servants, and friends turning away. He declares that his Redeemer lives. He wants his words preserved and someone to support his claim.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads Job’s Redeemer as Jesus Christ and invites reflection on resurrection.

passages.title: Zophar says wicked success ends quickly
passages.summary: Zophar describes stolen wealth turning into suffering. He says wicked people cannot keep their success. His argument depends on a link between wealth, guilt, and ruin that Job will dispute.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Zophar links wickedness with brief success. What evidence would challenge his claim?

passages.title: Job points to wicked people who prosper
passages.summary: Job describes wicked people growing old with safe homes and thriving children. He challenges his friends’ answers. Their rule fails to explain lives where wrongdoing and comfort appear together.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the contrast between wicked success and faithful suffering.

passages.title: Eliphaz names sins he assumes Job committed
passages.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of withholding food, clothing, and help. He urges Job to return to God. The accusations grow more specific, though Eliphaz supplies no account of witnessing them.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help.

passages.title: Job searches for God’s court
passages.summary: Job wants to present his case to God. He cannot find him, but insists he kept his commands. Job’s confidence about his conduct stands beside his fear of God’s power.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions.

passages.title: Job describes the suffering of the poor
passages.summary: Job describes stolen fields, hungry workers, and people without shelter. He asks why justice seems delayed. The argument widens beyond his own pain to people harmed by others.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how Restoration scripture helps readers think about suffering.

passages.title: Bildad questions human purity
passages.summary: Bildad says God rules above and even the stars lack purity before him. He compares people to worms. His brief answer offers no direct help with Job’s examples of injustice.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?

passages.title: Job describes power beyond human knowledge
passages.summary: Job first asks how Bildad has helped him. He describes God’s power over sky, sea, and death. Knowing that God is powerful does not settle their dispute about justice.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?

passages.title: Job holds to his innocence
passages.summary: Job refuses to admit the friends are right about him. He then describes the fate of oppressors. He rejects their verdict while continuing to discuss judgment against wrongdoing.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?

passages.title: Where can wisdom be found?
passages.summary: A poem describes miners finding hidden metals. It asks where wisdom lies and says God knows its way. Skill at finding treasure does not give people complete understanding.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?

passages.title: Job remembers respect and service
passages.summary: Job recalls public honor and his children nearby. He remembers helping widows and people in need. He connects his former standing with care for others.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?

passages.title: Job describes shame and unanswered cries
passages.summary: Job contrasts former respect with mockery and pain. He says his calls to God receive no answer. His changed treatment adds public humiliation to his physical suffering.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?

passages.title: Job gives his final defense
passages.summary: Job lists wrongs he says he avoided. He describes fairness toward servants, generosity, and welcome for strangers. He asks for a written charge and a chance to answer it.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him.

passages.title: Elihu begins after the others fall silent
passages.summary: Elihu becomes angry with Job and his three friends. He says youth does not prevent understanding. He waited for older speakers but now claims they failed to answer.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?

passages.title: Elihu says suffering can teach
passages.summary: Elihu says God speaks through dreams and pain. He describes rescue through a messenger and renewed health. This is Elihu’s explanation for suffering, given before God speaks.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?

passages.title: Elihu defends God’s justice
passages.summary: Elihu says God treats rich and poor without favor. He accuses Job of adding rebellion to sin. His defense of justice becomes another charge against Job.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?

passages.title: Elihu challenges Job’s complaint
passages.summary: Elihu says human choices affect other people. He claims pride prevents cries for help from being heard. He treats silence as a failure in the sufferer’s response.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?

passages.title: Elihu describes correction and the storm
passages.summary: Elihu says suffering opens people’s ears to instruction. He describes rain, clouds, and lightning. His speech moves from explaining human pain to describing God’s work in nature.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?

passages.title: Elihu asks Job to consider God’s works
passages.summary: Elihu describes thunder, snow, and changing weather. He asks whether Job understands their workings. His final questions prepare for the change from human debate to God’s speech.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?

passages.title: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
passages.summary: The Lord questions Job about earth, sea, dawn, weather, stars, and animals. The answer draws Job into a world much larger than his dispute.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth.

passages.title: The Lord describes wild animals
passages.summary: The Lord asks about goats, wild donkeys, oxen, ostriches, horses, hawks, and eagles. These creatures have strength and freedom that people cannot command.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view.

passages.title: Job falls silent and hears about behemoth
passages.summary: Job places his hand over his mouth. The Lord questions his judgment and describes behemoth’s strength. The creature’s power challenges Job’s ability to govern the world he questions.
passages.uncertainty: The poem names the Jordan. This marker does not locate Job’s home.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views.

passages.title: The Lord describes Leviathan
passages.summary: The Lord describes Leviathan’s scales, strength, and frightening breath. Human tools cannot subdue it. The poem presents power that exceeds human control.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?

passages.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
passages.summary: Job answers the Lord. The Lord rebukes the three friends. Job prays for them and receives renewed prosperity. The friends need the prayer of the man they accused. Job’s daughters receive an inheritance.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s prayer and renewed life with hope after loss.

events.detail: The accusations grow more specific, though Eliphaz supplies no account of witnessing them.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help.

events.title: Job searches for God’s court
events.summary: Job wants to present his case to God. He cannot find him, but insists he kept his commands.
events.detail: Job’s confidence about his conduct stands beside his fear of God’s power.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions.

events.title: Job describes the suffering of the poor
events.summary: Job describes stolen fields, hungry workers, and people without shelter. He asks why justice seems delayed.
events.detail: The argument widens beyond his own pain to people harmed by others.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how Restoration scripture helps readers think about suffering.

events.title: Bildad questions human purity
events.summary: Bildad says God rules above and even the stars lack purity before him. He compares people to worms.
events.detail: His brief answer offers no direct help with Job’s examples of injustice.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?

events.title: Job describes power beyond human knowledge
events.summary: Job first asks how Bildad has helped him. He describes God’s power over sky, sea, and death.
events.detail: Knowing that God is powerful does not settle their dispute about justice.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?

events.title: Job holds to his innocence
events.summary: Job refuses to admit the friends are right about him. He then describes the fate of oppressors.
events.detail: He rejects their verdict while continuing to discuss judgment against wrongdoing.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?

events.title: Where can wisdom be found?
events.summary: A poem describes miners finding hidden metals. It asks where wisdom lies and says God knows its way.
events.detail: Skill at finding treasure does not give people complete understanding.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?

events.title: Job remembers respect and service
events.summary: Job recalls public honor and his children nearby. He remembers helping widows and people in need.
events.detail: He connects his former standing with care for others.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?

events.title: Job describes shame and unanswered cries
events.summary: Job contrasts former respect with mockery and pain. He says his calls to God receive no answer.
events.detail: His changed treatment adds public humiliation to his physical suffering.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?

events.title: Job gives his final defense
events.summary: Job lists wrongs he says he avoided. He describes fairness toward servants, generosity, and welcome for strangers.
events.detail: He asks for a written charge and a chance to answer it.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him.

events.title: Elihu begins after the others fall silent
events.summary: Elihu becomes angry with Job and his three friends. He says youth does not prevent understanding.
events.detail: He waited for older speakers but now claims they failed to answer.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?

events.title: Elihu says suffering can teach
events.summary: Elihu says God speaks through dreams and pain. He describes rescue through a messenger and renewed health.
events.detail: This is Elihu’s explanation for suffering, given before God speaks.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?

events.title: Elihu defends God’s justice
events.summary: Elihu says God treats rich and poor without favor. He accuses Job of adding rebellion to sin.
events.detail: His defense of justice becomes another charge against Job.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?

events.title: Elihu challenges Job’s complaint
events.summary: Elihu says human choices affect other people. He claims pride prevents cries for help from being heard.
events.detail: He treats silence as a failure in the sufferer’s response.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?

events.title: Elihu describes correction and the storm
events.summary: Elihu says suffering opens people’s ears to instruction. He describes rain, clouds, and lightning.
events.detail: His speech moves from explaining human pain to describing God’s work in nature.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?

events.title: Elihu asks Job to consider God’s works
events.summary: Elihu describes thunder, snow, and changing weather. He asks whether Job understands their workings.
events.detail: His final questions prepare for the change from human debate to God’s speech.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?

events.title: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
events.summary: The Lord questions Job about earth, sea, dawn, weather, stars, and animals.
events.detail: The answer draws Job into a world much larger than his dispute.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth.

events.title: The Lord describes wild animals
events.summary: The Lord asks about goats, wild donkeys, oxen, ostriches, horses, hawks, and eagles.
events.detail: These creatures have strength and freedom that people cannot command.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view.

events.title: Job falls silent and hears about behemoth
events.summary: Job places his hand over his mouth. The Lord questions his judgment and describes behemoth’s strength.
events.detail: The creature’s power challenges Job’s ability to govern the world he questions.
events.uncertainty: The poem names the Jordan. This marker does not locate Job’s home.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views.

events.title: The Lord describes Leviathan
events.summary: The Lord describes Leviathan’s scales, strength, and frightening breath. Human tools cannot subdue it.
events.detail: The poem presents power that exceeds human control.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?

events.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
events.summary: Job answers the Lord. The Lord rebukes the three friends. Job prays for them and receives renewed prosperity.
events.detail: The friends need the prayer of the man they accused. Job’s daughters receive an inheritance.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s prayer and renewed life with hope after loss.

guides.title: Study Job
guides.description: Follow selected chapters through the book.

steps.title: Job loses his children and wealth
steps.text: Satan questions Job’s reasons for serving God. Four messengers report losses. Job mourns and worships. Job’s good life does not protect his family from disaster.

steps.title: Eliphaz names sins he assumes Job committed
steps.text: Eliphaz accuses Job of withholding food, clothing, and help. He urges Job to return to God. The accusations grow more specific, though Eliphaz supplies no account of witnessing them.

steps.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
steps.text: Job answers the Lord. The Lord rebukes the three friends. Job prays for them and receives renewed prosperity. The friends need the prayer of the man they accused. Job’s daughters receive an inheritance.
